name: tamserve
cost: Free and open source (Apache-2.0). SAM 3, needed for tracking by name, has its own licence.
works_with: Python 3.10+, NVIDIA GPUs, EdgeTAM, SAM 2.1 and SAM 3
short: Tracks objects on many live camera feeds at once with SAM 2 or EdgeTAM, sharing one copy of the model on one GPU or many.
what: tamserve is a serving engine for Meta's SAM 2.1 and EdgeTAM tracking models. Every camera shares one copy of the model, so on the README's RTX 4090 tests it uses far less GPU memory and runs faster than one copy per camera, with the same accuracy. You point at what to track with a box, clicks or a mask. A `Tracker` can also find things by name, such as "dog", using SAM 3.
who: Developers who need to know where things are in live video: sports graphics, warehouse analytics, robotics, lab or wildlife monitoring, annotation tools. It is a Python library with no app or camera handling of its own, so skip it if you do not write code.
needs: An NVIDIA GPU (it runs on a CPU, but far too slowly for live video)
An internet connection the first time a model loads
Your own code to read camera frames, for example with OpenCV
Optional: a Hugging Face account that has accepted Meta's SAM 3 licence, only for tracking by name

steps.title: Load the engine
steps.text: This loads EdgeTAM onto the GPU. The first time, it downloads the 54 MB model into `~/.cache/tamserve`.

steps.title: Track things in your loop
steps.text: Call `engine.step()` once per round with the newest frame from each camera. Pass a `Box` around each object only on the first call; the engine tracks it from there.

steps.title: Log in to Hugging Face
steps.text: Run this once, and accept Meta's licence on the facebook/sam3 page first. The 3.5 GB of weights download the first time a tracker starts.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Open the quickstart notebook from the README's Colab badge, or the tracking-by-name notebook, and run it before wiring up your own cameras.

watch: It downloads model weights the first time you load a model. SAM 3's weights are 3.5 GB, need a Hugging Face login and come under Meta's own licence, which is not Apache-2.0.
The first compiled start takes about 20 minutes. After that it takes about 95 seconds while PyTorch's cache is still there.
Every speed in the README comes from one RTX 4090. Older GPUs without bf16 support are much slower; on a free Colab T4 one SAM 3 look takes 3 seconds.
It only tracks forward in time, and each extra object adds about 2.4 ms to a round.
The DAVIS 2017 dataset used for accuracy scores is for research use, so check its licence before using it for anything else.
